facts.statement: The only known fossil of Unescoceratops is a partial left dentary known as holotype specimen TMP 95.12.6.
facts.quote: Unescoceratops is known only from the holotype specimen TMP 95.12.6, a partial left dentary.

facts.statement: Unescoceratops lived during the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 76.5 to 75 million years ago.
facts.quote: dating to the late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, about 76.5-75 million years ago.

facts.statement: Unescoceratops possessed the roundest teeth of all leptoceratopsids.
facts.quote: Its teeth were the roundest of all leptoceratopsids.

facts.statement: The genus Unescoceratops was first described by Michael J. Ryan, David C. Evans, Philip J. Currie, Caleb M. Brown, and Don Brinkman in 2012.
facts.quote: The genus Unescoceratops was first described by Michael J. Ryan, David C. Evans, Philip J. Currie, Caleb M. Brown and Don Brinkman in 2012

facts.statement: The generic name Unescoceratops means "UNESCO horned face" because the fossil was found in a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
facts.quote: The generic name means "UNESCO horned face", in reference to the fossil being found in an area designated as a World Heritage Site by the organization.

facts.statement: The specific epithet koppelhusae honors palynologist Eva Koppelhus, the wife of Philip J. Currie.
facts.quote: The specific epithet is named after Currie's wife, palynologist Eva Koppelhus.

facts.statement: Unescoceratops is classified as a leptoceratopsid and is the sister taxon to Gryphoceratops.
facts.quote: Unescoceratops has been classified as a leptoceratopsid and the sister taxa to Gryphoceratops, which was described in the same paper.

facts.statement: According to a cladogram proposed by Ryan and colleagues, Unescoceratops is currently considered one of the most advanced leptoceratopsids.
facts.quote: De momento se ha encontrado que es uno de los leptoceratópsidos más avanzados, según el cladograma propuesto por Ryan y colaboradores

facts.statement: The time range recorded for Unescoceratops in the Paleobiology Database spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Campanian (83.6 to 72.2 million years ago)
